stances.claim: The Constitution deems 'inviolable' the right against UNREASONABLE searches/seizures, with a search becoming reasonable as a rule only when ordered by a judge through a written search warrant satisfying six elements: (1) judge determines probable cause; (2) via personal examination; (3) of complainant and witnesses under oath; (4) place to be searched; (5) persons or things to be seized; (6) particularly described in the warrant.

Probable cause has no fixed formula but in general exists when 'facts and circumstances... could lead a reasonably discreet and prudent person to believe (1) that an offense had been committed and (2) that the items, articles or objects sought in connection with the said offense are in the place to be searched.'

Jurisprudence has carved out seven exceptions to the search-warrant requirement: (1) incident to lawful arrest; (2) plain view; (3) vehicle; (4) consent; (5) customs ports of entry/exit; (6) stop-and-frisk; (7) exigent and emergency circumstances.

At checkpoints, the vehicle-search exception permits only visual inspection by default -- drawing aside the curtain of a vacant vehicle, looking without touching, using a flashlight without opening doors -- and prohibits subjecting occupants to physical/body search. Extensive and intrusive search requires that the policemen (like judges) have probable cause PRIOR TO THE SEARCH that (1) a crime has been committed and (2) the article pertaining to that crime can be found in the vehicle.

Critically, an anonymous tip or verbal informant statement, standing alone, is not sufficient to constitute probable cause -- it must first be 'verified by the policemen through his/her own personal knowledge (not hearsay) prior to the search.' To repeat: 'a tip, standing alone, is not sufficient to constitute probable cause.'

Citizens have a self-help script: bring hard copies of this and last Sunday's columns; assert rights firmly but peacefully (not forcefully) -- because if they resist forcefully they may be deemed to have waived their rights and consented to the search under Exception 4, after which 'courts will not be able to help them.' Officers who conduct extensive searches without prior probable cause can be held 'criminally, civilly, and administratively liable now or in the future.'

notable_anecdotes: The 'To be understood by lay persons' lead-in -- converting CJ's column into an explicit civic primer rather than legal-academic exposition, an unusual register-marker.
The capitalization of UNREASONABLE, PROBABLE CAUSE, PERSONAL, and PRIOR TO THE SEARCH throughout the column -- typographic emphasis preserving the operative terms in a citizen-instruction frame.

The six-element search-warrant test enumerated with judge-liability tail ('A judge who does not follow them may be sued in, and administratively sanctioned, by the Court') -- making the test enforceable not just procedural.

The four-step visual-inspection list -- draw aside curtain, look around without touching, use flashlight without opening doors, NOT subject occupants to body search -- operational specificity equipping ordinary readers with a checklist they can apply at a checkpoint.
The 'tip standing alone' rule emphasized with 'To repeat' -- CJ's rare deliberate repetition, marking the rule he most wants citizens (and rogue officers) to internalize.

The bring-the-column-to-the-checkpoint advice -- 'citizens may bring a hard copy of this and last Sunday's columns to guide them (and the law-abiding policemen)' -- making the column a literal piece of legal self-defense equipment.

The waiver-trap warning embedded in citizen advice -- 'they should assert their rights firmly but peacefully (not forcefully). Otherwise, they may be deemed to have waived them' -- the precise procedural pitfall framed as practical caution.
The 'now or in the future' tail to the officer-liability warning -- leaving the temporal door open for accountability beyond the immediate political cycle.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes a civic primer on how police and military officers should conduct, and how citizens should regard, pandemic-era checkpoints set up to safeguard security, safety, and health. He builds on the prior week's column featuring People v. Sapla (Aug. 19, 2020, ably penned by Justice Alfredo Benjamin S. Caguioa). The constitutional baseline: the right against UNREASONABLE searches and seizures is 'inviolable,' and a search/seizure becomes reasonable as a rule only when ordered by a judge through a written search warrant satisfying six elements -- (1) the judge determines probable cause, (2) via personal examination, (3) of the complainant and witnesses under oath, (4) with the place to be searched and (5) the persons or things to be seized (6) particularly described in the warrant; a judge failing these may be sued and administratively sanctioned. Probable cause has no fixed formula but in general exists when 'facts and circumstances... could lead a reasonably discreet and prudent person to believe (1) that an offense had been committed and (2) that the items, articles or objects sought in connection with the said offense are in the place to be searched.' Jurisprudence has carved seven exceptions to the warrant requirement: (1) incident to lawful arrest, (2) plain view, (3) vehicle, (4) consent, (5) customs ports of entry/exit, (6) stop-and-frisk, (7) exigent and emergency circumstances. He focuses on the third -- vehicle search (boat, car, bus, truck, tricycle) -- which permits as routine only 'visual inspection': (1) drawing aside the curtain of a vacant vehicle, (2) looking without touching, (3) using a flashlight without opening doors, and (4) NOT subjecting occupants to physical or body search. To conduct an 'extensive and intrusive search' beyond visual inspection, the policemen 'must have PROBABLE CAUSE to believe PRIOR TO THE SEARCH that (1) a crime had been committed and (2) the article or object (usually prohibited drugs) pertaining to the crime... can be found in the vehicle.' Critically, the police 'cannot search a vehicle and the occupants thereof on the sole basis of an anonymous tip or a verbal statement by an informant'; the tip must be verified through the officer's own personal knowledge (not hearsay) before the search. 'To repeat, a tip, standing alone, is not sufficient to constitute probable cause.' Citizens have a practical self-help script: bring a hard copy of this and last Sunday's columns to checkpoints; assert rights 'firmly but peacefully (not forcefully).' If they resist forcefully they may be deemed to have waived their rights and consented to the search under Exception 4, after which 'courts will not be able to help them.' Without judge-issued search warrants, police and military officers at checkpoints can conduct only visual inspections; conducting an extensive search or seizure without first determining probable cause exposes them to 'criminal, civil, and administrative' liability -- 'now or in the future.'
